youtube.baslik: Real-Ear-to-Coupler Difference (RECD) in Children | Lesson 192 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
Why does the same hearing aid produce a louder sound in an infant's ear? In this lesson we cover the real-ear-to-coupler difference (RECD), how it is measured, predicted values by age, and simulated real-ear measurement in the coupler using the RECD.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: American Academy of Audiology, Clinical Practice Guidelines: Pediatric Amplification (2013); Bagatto et al. (2005), Clinical protocols for hearing instrument fitting in the Desired Sensation Level method, Trends in Amplification; Bagatto et al. (2002), Journal of the American Academy of Audiology; Martin, Munro and Langer (1997), British Journal of Audiology; Dillon, Hearing Aids.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn why the same hearing aid produces a much louder sound in an infant's ear.
We will cover the real-ear-to-coupler difference, or RECD, how it is measured, and the predicted values by age.
The pressure a sound creates in the ear canal depends on the size of the volume it is delivered into.
When the same amount of sound energy goes into a small volume, it creates a higher sound pressure than in a large one.
In infants the ear canal is both shorter and narrower, and the volume left in front of the earmold is very small.
So the same hearing aid setting produces a markedly higher sound level in an infant's ear than in an adult's.
The difference is especially large at high frequencies and varies from person to person.
A fitting that ignores this difference can give the child more sound than needed, even uncomfortable sound.

maddeler.metin: Children do not sit still for long
Fitting can be done in the coupler
Thresholds converted to ear canal SPL
Target and output on one scale

cumleler: In adults, output is verified directly with real-ear measurement, but a young child will not sit still through a long measurement.
What is more, working for a long time with a measurement loudspeaker in front of an infant is often not possible.
The solution is to find a correction for the child's own ear with a brief measurement and do the fitting in the test box, in a coupler.
The same correction is also used to convert dB HL thresholds obtained with insert earphones into dB SPL in the child's ear canal.
A coupler is a small measurement cavity of standard volume used to measure a hearing aid's output.
This way threshold, prescriptive target and aid output can be compared on the same screen, on the scale of the child's own ear canal.
The real-ear-to-coupler difference, or RECD, is the difference between two measurements.

cumleler.yazi: First, a sound is delivered through an insert earphone into a standard 2 cc coupler, and the resulting sound pressure level is measured.

cumleler: Then the same sound is delivered with the same earphone into the child's ear canal, and the level there is measured with a probe tube.
The level measured in the coupler is subtracted from the level measured in the ear canal.
This difference at each frequency is the RECD; the larger it is, the more sound pressure the ear canal produces compared with the coupler.
For example, if 82 dB SPL is measured in the ear canal and 72 dB SPL in the coupler at 2000 Hz, the RECD at that frequency is 10 dB.

notlar.metin: Probe tip a few mm beyond

cumleler: For the measurement, the probe tube is placed in the ear canal first.
Then sound is delivered from the insert earphone through a foam tip or the child's own earmold.
The tip of the probe tube should extend at least a few millimeters beyond the end of the foam tip or earmold.
The measurement usually takes only a few seconds, so it can be done even in a sleeping infant or one sitting on a lap.
Using the same type of coupling, that is, the same foam tip or earmold, for threshold testing and RECD measurement is recommended.
The coupler type also matters; measurement systems convert between different couplers in software.
When the earmold changes or the child grows, the RECD should be measured again.
For infants, the best moment for the measurement is sleep after a feed.
Older children can be measured on a parent's lap while kept busy with a toy or a video.
Because crying, talking and sucking movements can change the level in the ear canal, wait for a calm moment.
Before the measurement, look in the ear canal with an otoscope; if there is wax or discharge, the measurement is postponed.
Because sound comes directly from the insert earphone, loudspeaker position and head direction do not affect the result.
For an experienced clinician, the RECD is often the shortest step of the whole appointment.
This graph shows example RECD values measured with a foam tip in two age groups.
The RECD generally increases with frequency; it is larger at high frequencies.
In infants, values are markedly higher than in children over two years of age.
In this example, the RECD at 4000 Hz is about 17 dB in the first months and about 9 dB over two years of age.
As the ear canal grows, the RECD decreases and approaches adult values at around five years of age.
However, even among infants of the same age, differences of more than a few decibels can be seen.
When the RECD cannot be measured, average values calculated for age are used; this is called the predicted RECD.
Predicted values are largest in the first months, because the ear canal is smallest then.
Between one and two years of age the ear canal grows quickly and the RECD decreases.
Predicted values shrink with age and approach adult values at around five years of age.
Measurement systems suggest these values automatically, based on the child's date of birth.

cumleler.yazi: In adults too, the ear canal forms a smaller volume than the 2 cc coupler, so the RECD is positive at most frequencies.

maddeler.metin: An average does not represent individuals
If not measurable, an age-appropriate average

cumleler.yazi: The American Academy of Audiology's 2013 pediatric amplification guideline recommends measuring the child's RECD whenever possible.
cumleler.ses: The American Academy of Audiology's twenty thirteen pediatric amplification guideline recommends measuring the child's RECD whenever possible.

cumleler: This is because, especially in the first months, individual values can differ greatly from the average.
In an ear that lies a few decibels below or above the average, a fitting based on predicted values will be wrong.
If measurement is not possible, age-appropriate predicted values or recently measured values can be used.
The guideline notes that these values may be less accurate, so measurement should be done at the first suitable appointment.

adimlar.metin: dB SPL in the ear canal

cumleler: A child's thresholds are usually obtained in dB HL with insert earphones.
Using the RECD, these thresholds are converted to dB SPL in the child's ear canal.

cumleler.yazi: Starting from these values, the Desired Sensation Level method, DSL v5, calculates the targets to reach in the ear canal in dB SPL.
cumleler.ses: Starting from these values, the Desired Sensation Level method, DSL version 5, calculates the targets to reach in the ear canal in dB SPL.

cumleler: The aid is measured in the test box; adding the RECD to the output measured in the coupler gives the predicted output in the child's ear.
Because the measurement is made in a coupler rather than in the ear, this method is called simulated real-ear measurement.
This way the child takes part only in the few-second RECD measurement; the rest of the fitting is done in the test box.

cumleler.yazi: Now let us look at an example: the navy curve is the aid's output measured in the 2 cc coupler.

cumleler: The red curve is the level expected in the ear canal when this child's RECD values are added to the same output.
The difference is a few decibels at low frequencies, but exceeds 15 dB at high frequencies.
The dashed line is the prescriptive target; the level expected in the ear is quite close to target.
Had the same fitting been done by looking at coupler values, the child's ear would have received sound well above target.
This is exactly where the value of the RECD lies: it puts the small ear at the center of the fitting.
A ventilation tube or perforation adds the middle ear volume to the measurement, and the low-frequency RECD drops markedly.
Studies have reported low-frequency RECD about 15 dB lower in children with ventilation tubes than in their peers.
A loose earmold or leakage around the edge of the foam tip also lowers values at low frequencies.
As the child grows and earmolds are renewed, the RECD changes; a fitting based on an old value is misleading.
The coupler used must be selected correctly in the measurement and in the software; otherwise the values shift.

sahneler.metin: If you see an unexpectedly low or negative low-frequency RECD, think of leakage and the eardrum first: a loose tip, a ventilation tube or a perforation. Interpret accordingly.
cumleler: A tip from the field: if you see an unexpectedly low, even negative, RECD at low frequencies, question the measurement first.
A foam tip or earmold that does not sit fully causes leakage and low values at low frequencies.
If the tip is fine, check the file and otoscopy for a ventilation tube or a perforation in the tympanic membrane.
In such an ear the measured value should be used instead of average values, because the ear really does behave differently.
Note the finding in the file; when the tube comes out, the RECD should be measured again.

maddeler.metin: Small ear canal, high sound pressure
Coupler output plus RECD: ear estimate

cumleler: In this lesson we saw that a small ear canal creates a higher sound pressure with the same hearing aid.
The RECD is found by subtracting the level measured in the coupler from the level measured in the ear canal for the same signal.
Guidelines recommend a measured RECD; predicted values are used only when measurement is not possible.
Adding the RECD to the output measured in the coupler predicts the sound level that will occur in the child's ear.

sahneler.soru: At 4000 Hz, coupler output is 85 dB and RECD 14 dB. Expected level in the ear?
sahneler.aciklama: Expected level in the ear = coupler output + RECD: _85 + 14 = 99 dB SPL_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: at 4000 Hz, the output measured in the coupler is 85 dB SPL and the RECD is 14 dB. What level is expected in the ear canal?

cumleler: The correct answer is C: 99 dB SPL.
The expected level in the ear canal is found by adding the RECD to the coupler output: 85 plus 14, that is, 99 dB SPL.
